opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly I think the cost is easy to underestimate if you just look at the final paper. The headline result is this one plot, the time horizon growing exponentially, doubling roughly every seven months, and it looks simple. But a lot of work sits underneath it.

The biggest cost, I'd say, is the human baselining. To say a model can do tasks that take a human an hour, you need to know how long those tasks actually take skilled people. That means recruiting experienced engineers, getting them to sit down and actually do the tasks in comparable conditions, and dealing with everything that goes wrong: people who get stuck, people who fail, people who take wildly different amounts of time. That's expensive in money and in coordination effort. Then we had to decide how to treat failed attempts and how to aggregate times, and each of those choices took real thought.

Then there's building the task suites. Some tasks came from existing work like RE-Bench and our earlier HCAST suite, and we added shorter software-engineering tasks to cover the low end. Writing tasks that are well specified, that have reliable automatic scoring, and that resist cheating or shortcuts is slow, careful work. A task that's subtly broken can quietly corrupt your measurements.

Running the models is real but comparatively modest compute. The more expensive part is the people-time: building agent scaffolds, debugging runs, and reading transcripts to check whether a failure reflects the model's ability or just something dumb in the environment.

So the way I think about it: it was a substantial investment for an organization our size, many person-months across several people. I think it was worth it, because the output is a single metric that is fairly interpretable and lets you compare models across years of progress. That's rare. Most benchmarks saturate and then tell you nothing, and the time horizon framing gives you something you can extrapolate, with all the appropriate caveats.

The flip side is that it's not cheap to keep up to date. As models get better, you need longer tasks, and longer tasks are much more expensive to baseline. Getting a human to do a forty-hour task several times over is a very different proposition than a five-minute one. So one thing we think about is how to make this sustainable, maybe by leaning more on task-length estimates or other methods instead of full baselines for every task. Each shortcut introduces its own uncertainty, though.

r001.rationale: The response says some tasks came from the existing RE-Bench project, but it does not explain that the paper’s cost depends on whether RE-Bench’s separate project costs are included.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's actually something I think about a fair amount, because the headline result of that paper is pretty simple to state — this sort of doubling-every-seven-months trend in the length of tasks AI systems can do — and I think people sometimes assume that something that clean must have been cheap to produce. And it really wasn't.

The way I'd break it down is there are a few distinct cost centers. The first and probably the biggest is the task suite itself. You need a large set of tasks spanning a huge range of difficulties, from things that take a human a few seconds up to things that take many hours, and every one of those tasks needs to be well-specified, have a reliable scoring mechanism, and not be trivially gameable. Building tasks like that is slow, careful work, and a lot of it ends up on the cutting-room floor because the task turns out to be ambiguous or broken in some way you didn't anticipate.

The second is the human baselining. The whole framing of "time horizon" depends on knowing how long these tasks actually take people, so you have to pay skilled humans — in a lot of cases people with real software engineering or research backgrounds — to sit down and do the tasks under reasonably controlled conditions. That's expensive per data point, and you need enough data points to get meaningful estimates, especially on the long tasks where any single baseline could take someone most of a day.

And then the third is just running the models, which is the part people tend to focus on but which I'd actually say is the smallest piece relative to the others. Running frontier agents on multi-hour tasks does burn a lot of tokens, but compute is comparatively cheap next to person-hours of expert labor.

So in total, you're talking about something that's a substantial fraction of a small organization's annual effort. I think that's worth being honest about, because it has implications for who can do this kind of work. It's not something an individual researcher can replicate over a weekend, and it means the field is somewhat dependent on a small number of groups having the resources and the willingness to invest in measurement infrastructure that doesn't itself produce a flashy capability.

My view is that it's clearly worth it. The alternative to spending that money is flying blind on one of the most important questions in the field — how fast is this actually moving? — and I'd much rather have an expensive, imperfect measurement than an unfounded vibe. But I do think there's a real question about how you make the next version cheaper, whether that's through better tooling for task creation, smarter ways of estimating human baselines without running every one, or just accumulating a task bank that gets amortized over many rounds of evaluation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task-suite, human-baselining, and model-running costs, but does not mention RE-Bench or say that the cost depends on whether that separate project is counted.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish the cost of running the evaluations from the cost of developing the methodology and building the infrastructure. Running the models is one component, but there’s also a lot of human work in constructing tasks, checking that they’re meaningful, getting human baselines, and figuring out how to analyze the results.

There’s also a question of what you attribute to this particular paper. If you count all the work that made it possible, that’s a different number from the marginal cost of adding another model to the plot. I don’t have a precise accounting to give you, but I think that distinction matters when thinking about how expensive it would be to keep these measurements updated.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes broad enabling work from the paper’s marginal costs, but it does not say that attribution depends on whether the separate RE-Bench project is counted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish the marginal cost of running the evaluations from the cost of getting to the point where you can run them. There’s the compute, but there’s also a lot of work in building the tasks, checking that they’re meaningful, measuring how long they take humans, and making sure the evaluation is actually telling you what you think it is.

And then there’s a question of accounting: how much of that work do you charge to this particular paper? If you build infrastructure that you’ll use for lots of subsequent evaluations, treating all of that as the cost of one paper seems misleading. But just reporting the cost of the final runs would also leave out a lot. So I’d be hesitant to give a single number without being clear about which of those things we’re counting.

r001.rationale: The response says reusable infrastructure may or may not be charged to the paper, but it never mentions RE-Bench or connects the accounting question to that project.
